target.repo: neem-square (local copy, not a git repository)

findings.issue: The court order and government intimation runbook sets a removal target of 36 hours from the order reaching the inbox, and says orders arriving outside rota hours are picked up on the next working day. The rule gives 3 hours from receipt. Orders sent by post go to the Singapore office, which scans post once a week (line 8). The runbook was last reviewed in August 2025, before G.S.R. 775(E) and G.S.R. 120(E).
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the target as 3 hours from receipt, measured from arrival at any channel, with no next-working-day carve-out. Route postal orders to an address in India that is opened daily, or tell senders to use the monitored email route. Re-review the runbook against the current rule 3(1)(d) text.

findings.issue: The legal-orders rota, which receives court orders and government intimations, covers Monday to Friday, 10:00 to 18:00 IST, and is reached by email, not by pager. An order that arrives at 21:00 on a Friday is not read until Monday morning: about 61 hours, against a 3-hour clock. The admin action (services/moderation/takedown.py remove_on_order) and the audit log exist; the people who trigger them are not on call.
findings.recommendation: Make the legal-orders route 24x7 with pager escalation, as the safety-priority and lea-liaison rotas already are, or give the on-call Trust and Safety rota authority to act on an order that meets the runbook checks and have counsel review afterwards.

findings.issue: NCII_SLA is 24 hours; the rule gives 2 hours from the complaint. Intimate imagery and impersonation complaints, including morphed images, take their due time from this constant (services/grievance/intake.py line 19). PAGE_AFTER on line 8 re-pages at 12 hours, which is also past the 2-hour deadline.
findings.recommendation: Set NCII_SLA to 2 hours and PAGE_AFTER well inside it (for example 30 minutes). The queue is already paged 24x7 through the safety-priority rota, so the change is to the constants and the reviewer staffing behind that pager.

findings.issue: The grievance page gives a role mailbox (grievance@) and the report form, but names no Grievance Officer and gives no contact details for one. As a significant social media intermediary, Neem Square must also have a Resident Grievance Officer doing the rule 3(2) job: no officer is named anywhere in the reviewed pages, and nothing says the officer is an employee resident in India.
findings.recommendation: Name the Grievance Officer on the grievance page, with their designation, a contact email and the complaint mechanism, and state that they are an employee resident in India. /draft writes a first draft of this page.

findings.issue: The grievance details are three clicks from the home page: Home, then Help in the footer, then Legal and safety, then Grievance redressal (web/templates/help.html line 9, web/templates/legal_index.html line 5). The report form is two clicks away. The footer, present on every page, has no grievance link, and the Contact page sends complaints to Help. The rule asks for the details on the home page or a page directly reachable from it.
findings.recommendation: Add a "Grievance redressal" link to the footer pointing at /help/legal/grievance, and put the Grievance Officer's name and contact on that page.

findings.issue: resolve_days is 15; the rule gives 7 days from receipt. Every complaint outside the fast-track and removal categories (copyright, account, other) gets its due date from this value (services/grievance/intake.py line 22), and the escalation job fires 12 hours before that due date.
findings.recommendation: Set resolve_days to 7.

findings.issue: content_removal_hours is 72; the rule gives 36 hours for a complaint asking for removal of content under rule 3(1)(b), other than sub-clauses (i), (iv) and (xi). Community Guidelines and synthetic media complaints take their due time from this value (services/grievance/intake.py line 21).
findings.recommendation: Set content_removal_hours to 36.

findings.cross_reference: DPDP Act s.8(7) and s.12(3) except retention needed to comply with a law in force (in force from May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E)): see Vigil. What may be kept after day 180, and which records the rule reaches, are questions for counsel.
findings.issue: The nightly purge deletes posts removed by moderation 30 days after removal: the media renditions, the moderation_events rows and comments, then the post itself. The rule requires removed information and its associated records to be preserved for 180 days. Only the audit_log row survives. The same purge also deletes moderation_events that the monthly compliance report counts, so on the first day of a 31-day month part of the previous month's proactive removals are gone before jobs/compliance_report.py runs.
findings.recommendation: Set KEEP_REMOVED to 180 days, or move removed posts, media and moderation records to a preservation store with a 180-day hold and an override for court or agency holds, and delete from the live tables only.

findings.cross_reference: DPDP Act s.8(7) and s.12(3) except retention needed to comply with a law in force (in force from May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E)): see Vigil. What may be kept after day 180, and which records the rule reaches, are questions for counsel.
findings.issue: The nightly job deletes signup_records (the registration information: email, phone, date of birth, signup IP and time) and the user row 30 days after an account is closed. The rule requires registration information to be retained for 180 days after cancellation or withdrawal. The Privacy Policy promises deletion within 30 days (web/legal/privacy.md line 17); its content is DPDP work and was not reviewed here.
findings.recommendation: Keep signup_records for 180 days after closed_at, out of the live tables if needed, before deleting them. Bring the Privacy Policy's retention statement into line, with counsel.

findings.issue: image_to_image, the Imagine path that edits an uploaded photo ("change what someone is wearing or doing"), calls neither the prompt filter nor the output classifier. text_to_image calls both (lines 21 and 23), and both fail closed when the classifier is down. The unfiltered path is the one where a real person's photo enters, which is where non-consensual intimate imagery and deceptive depictions of real people come from.
findings.recommendation: Call safety.check_prompt on the instruction and safety.check_output on the result in image_to_image, as text_to_image does, and add a check on the source image for a real, identifiable person combined with the blocked topics.

findings.issue: The creators.clean_export flag (config/features.yaml line 14, enabled) lets verified creators post Imagine images without the burned-in "AI-generated" label: _finish skips burn_in when the flag is on and the user is a verified creator. The rule requires the label on every piece of synthetic media and forbids enabling its suppression. Provenance metadata is still written on this path.
findings.recommendation: Remove the clean_export exemption so every Imagine output gets the label, and turn the flag off in config/features.yaml.

findings.issue: prepare_for_feed runs on every post, including Imagine results (api/posts.py line 15), and drops all EXIF, XMP and IPTC metadata. That strips the provenance metadata services/imagine/provenance.py writes at generation, including the generator id and the per-asset unique identifier, before the image reaches the CDN. The burned-in label survives; the metadata does not. The same step strips provenance that arrived with uploaded files made elsewhere; that part rests on reading rule 3(3) to reach hosts, which the catalog note leaves to counsel.
findings.recommendation: Keep the privacy strip for GPS and device fields, but preserve the neem: provenance fields (and C2PA manifests on uploads) through orient, resize and WebP encoding, and re-write them on each rendition if the encoder drops them.

findings.issue: The only postal address published is the Singapore parent's (Neem Square Pte. Ltd.), and the page says legal notices should be sent there. No physical contact address in India is published. The officers are described as based in Bengaluru, but no address is given.
findings.recommendation: Publish a physical contact address in India for receiving communications on the Contact page, and point legal notices to it.

findings.issue: The new-post form asks for a photo, caption, audience and comments setting, but not whether the content is synthetically generated. The posts table stores no declaration (db/schema.sql lines 19 to 31), and nothing in the upload path detects synthetic media or reads provenance on upload. Only Imagine output is labelled, and that labelling does not cover outside uploads.
findings.recommendation: Add a required "made or edited with AI" declaration to the upload form and store it on the post; check uploads for provenance metadata (C2PA, XMP) or with a classifier; label declared or detected content in the feed.

findings.issue: Step 1 of the runbook checks the issuing court or authority, the URLs named and the legal basis. It does not check the conditions the rule sets for a government intimation to give actual knowledge: in writing and reasoned, from an officer of at least Joint Secretary rank (Director where no such rank is appointed; DIG for the police) authorised by order in writing, and stating the nature of the unlawful act. What to do with an intimation that falls short is a question for counsel, per the catalog note.
findings.recommendation: Add a checklist step that reads each government intimation against every rule 3(1)(d)(ii) condition and records the result in the orders register, with escalation to counsel when one is missing. Do not hold the 3-hour clock on that escalation without counsel's instruction.

findings.issue: The terms reminder runs on cron "0 9 15 1 *": 09:00 IST on 15 January, once a year. The rule requires the reminder at least once every three months. The comment beside the entry says only "periodic".
findings.recommendation: Change the schedule to at least quarterly, for example "0 9 15 1,4,7,10 *".

findings.issue: The reminder carries only limb (i): content removal and suspension or closure of the account. It does not say that a user responsible for unlawful content may face penalty or punishment (limb ii), or that offences that must be reported will be reported to the authorities (limb iii). Limb (iii) is unconfirmed against the gazette: the catalog follows the corrigendum G.S.R. 148(E), read only as a footnote. The reminder also carries none of the rule 3(1)(ca) warnings on synthetic content, which are read with this notice. It is in English only.
findings.recommendation: Add limbs (ii) and (iii) and the rule 3(1)(ca) warnings to the reminder body, and offer it in the user's chosen language where the product supports Indian languages.

findings.issue: The Imagine section of the Terms says only that users should use Imagine responsibly, not use it to mislead people, and that use may be limited. The Community Guidelines ask users to keep the AI-generated mark. Neither tells users that making unlawful synthetic content may attract penalty under the laws listed, or that a contravention may lead to removal, suspension or termination, disclosure of identity to a victim complainant in accordance with law, and mandatory reporting.
findings.recommendation: Add both rule 3(1)(ca) warnings to the Imagine section of the Terms and to the Imagine screen, and carry them in the three-monthly reminder.

findings.issue: remove_for_policy removes content for a Community Guidelines breach found by a moderator or the classifier straight away, with no notice to the uploader beforehand and no reasons sent. No dispute or reinstatement route for the uploader was found in the reviewed material. The copyright path (line 28) notifies the owner only after removal.
findings.recommendation: Before a rule 3(1)(b) removal on the platform's own accord, notify the uploader with the action and reasons, give a dispute and reinstatement route, and have the Resident Grievance Officer oversee it.

findings.issue: No step for complying with a Grievance Appellate Committee order, or for uploading a report of that compliance to the website, was found in the reviewed material. The runbooks cover court orders and law enforcement requests only; the /transparency template was not supplied.
findings.recommendation: Add a runbook step for Committee orders: who receives them, who implements them, and where the compliance report is published.

findings.issue: No hash matching or classifier on upload for depictions of rape or child sexual abuse, and no matching of re-uploads against content removed under rule 3(1)(d), was found in the reviewed material. The upload pipeline only orients, strips metadata and resizes. The compliance report counts removals tagged "policy:auto", so some automated tooling may exist outside the reviewed code. No review record for automated tools was found.
findings.recommendation: Add hash matching (for example against a CSAM hash list) and a classifier on upload, keep hashes of content removed under rule 3(1)(d) to catch identical re-uploads, show a notice to users who try to reach matched content, and record a periodic review of the tools.

findings.issue: Court orders and government notices are received by the Legal rota at legal@, not by the Grievance Officer, and are acknowledged only after removal (step 5, line 16). Postal orders go to Singapore and are scanned weekly (line 8). The runbook does have a monitored address and an acknowledgement step, so the gap is partial.
findings.recommendation: Name the Grievance Officer as a recipient of orders and notices in the runbook (copied on the legal@ route), and acknowledge receipt on arrival rather than after removal.

not_checked: DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025 (use Vigil)
IT Rules Part III (digital media publishers) and rule 5
Online gaming provisions: rule 3(1)(b)(ix)-(x), rule 4(10)-(13), rules 4A to 4C
Rule 3(1)(i), (k), (l), (m), (n): security practices, CERT-In reporting, accessibility, constitutional rights
Rule 4(2) first originator, rule 4(3) advertised content, rule 4(7) voluntary verification
Whether a particular court order or government intimation is valid under rule 3(1)(d): nodal checks that a process exists to read one against the rule, not any actual order
RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI and other sector rules
Blocking orders under section 69A of the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009
Any amendment or corrigendum notified after G.S.R. 120(E) of 10 February 2026. A draft Second Amendment was published on 30 March 2026; whether it has been notified was not checked
Whether the product is an intermediary in law: the classification records the user's answer and what the code shows
E-Commerce Rules grievance duties: the classification carries no ecom or ecom-seller tag (the footer Merch link opens a third-party shop), so /ecom did not run
Live site: none given, and the app has none. Every finding comes from the repository
Whether the Ministry has made a rule 6 order for this product: not stated; the ssmi tag rests on the 62 lakh user count in the README

Material referenced but not supplied: web/templates/base.html, transparency.html, imagine.html and post_card.html; the /help/imagine, /help/legal/law-enforcement, /help/legal/copyright and /help/report/status pages; the signup screen and app settings; the Android app; the services/imagine label, classifier and model modules; services/media xmp and codec; the copyright notice template; account suspension code paths
Language of the documents and reminder: all are in English only, and the material does not say whether the product is offered in Indian languages or lets users choose one

Whether the compliance report counts only complaints from users in India, as its heading says: the queries in jobs/compliance_report.py do not filter by country, and the rule text read does not require it

Rule 3(1)(cb) account action: users.status allows suspension, but the code that suspends an account, discloses identity to a victim or makes a mandatory report was not in the reviewed material. No finding was filed
disclaimer: nodal is compliance tooling, not legal advice. It reports gaps visible in the material reviewed and never certifies compliance. Have a qualified lawyer check every finding before relying on it.
